items.title: Bountiful Roebuck Bay
items.short_description: Tidal and seasonal shifts leave their mark on this crescent-shaped, productive bay in Western Australia's Kimberley region.
items.abstract: Tidal and seasonal shifts leave their mark on this crescent-shaped, productive bay in Western Australia's Kimberley region. Among those places is Roebuck Bay, a crescent-shaped feature in the Kimberley region of Western Australia. But the large range at Roebuck Bay is mostly a consequence of northwestern Australia's unusually wide, shallow continental shelf, which helps amplify tides as they approach the coast. The consistent spacing of the tidal creeks is likely not a tidal effect; it appears to be influenced by the regular spacing of linear dunes in the broader region, as seen in the plains to the east. The bay's dramatic tidal and seasonal changes are striking from above, and they also support a bounty of life on the ground.

items.title: El Niño Alters Marine Life in the Pacific
items.short_description: Satellite measurements of chlorophyll at the sea surface signal shifts in the ocean’s nutrient supplies in mid-2026.
items.abstract: Satellite measurements of chlorophyll at the sea surface signal shifts in the ocean’s nutrient supplies in mid-2026. The maps above show chlorophyll-a concentrations—the pigment present in most phytoplankton —as observed by the OCI (Ocean Color Instrument) on NASA’s PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite. That’s because during an El Niño, easterly equatorial trade winds weaken, the warm surface layer of the ocean extends deeper, and the upwelling of cool, nutrient-rich water that typically fuels phytoplankton growth is suppressed. Although the disruptions to marine life can be severe, a post-El Niño “chlorophyll rebound,” with higher-than-normal concentrations in the equatorial Pacific, can occur. To better understand effects on life in the ocean, researchers hope to use PACE data to gauge the responses of specific phytoplankton communities to El Niño. And the possibilities extend beyond the marine realm, the scientists note.

items.title: Sensing the Poles’ Hidden Heat
items.short_description: New animations from NASA's PREFIRE mission reveal two years of seasonal temperature swings at the Arctic and Antarctic.
items.abstract: New animations from NASA's PREFIRE mission reveal two years of seasonal temperature swings at the Arctic and Antarctic. Satellite data from a mission measuring infrared energy reveal just how differently—and how dramatically—surface temperatures swing across two full years at the poles. Atmospheric and ocean circulation carries excess heat absorbed in the tropics toward the poles, where it radiates away to space, helping regulate the planet’s temperature. “By measuring invisible heat radiating from Earth's coldest places, PREFIRE is helping scientists understand why the poles are changing so rapidly, and what those changes might mean for the rest of the planet,” said Chad Greene, a glaciologist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Maps courtesy of Chad Greene, NASA/JPL, using data from NASA’s PREFIRE mission.

items.title: How the Tide Turns at the Mouth of the Elbe
items.short_description: The ocean’s ebbs and flows reveal dynamic tidal flats and a well-traveled shipping route along the coast of Germany.
items.abstract: The ocean’s ebbs and flows reveal dynamic tidal flats and a well-traveled shipping route along the coast of Germany. One of the major rivers of Europe, the Elbe flows more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) across the continent before reaching the North Sea. These dynamic tidal flats are a boon to biodiversity while sometimes posing challenges for those navigating its waters and for communities living along its shores. The Elbe’s mouth also provides access to the Kiel Canal, which connects the North Sea and Baltic Sea and is the world’s busiest human-made waterway navigable by seagoing ships. In addition, early data from NASA’s SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography) satellite has demonstrated the potential to accurately measure water levels around complex coastlines and to improve tidal models.

items.title: The Paradox of Lençóis Maranhenses National Park
items.short_description: The coastal dune field in Brazil looks like a desert but fills with freshwater lagoons every year.
items.abstract: The coastal dune field in Brazil looks like a desert but fills with freshwater lagoons every year. The coastal dune system in Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil is among the most surreal landscapes on Earth. At first glance, the park looks like a desert, but it is far from it. From that perspective, the sweeping curves of the largest coastal dune field in South America resemble a rumpled, white bedsheet. The dune field exists because of the rare convergence of geologic and climatic conditions. Landsat images, meanwhile, show the dune field at Lençóis Maranhenses has extended westward by about 0.5 kilometers between 1986 and 2026 in some areas due to the conveyor belt of dunes running inland from the coastline.

items.title: Smoke Streams Across Eastern Washington
items.short_description: Wildland fires in early August 2026 pushed air quality to unhealthy levels, destroyed hundreds of structures, and triggered mandatory evacuations in Spokane.
items.abstract: Wildland fires in early August 2026 pushed air quality to unhealthy levels, destroyed hundreds of structures, and triggered mandatory evacuations in Spokane. The start of August 2026 saw ongoing and new wildland fires burning in eastern Washington. The smoke from these and other fires poured east-northeast across the state and into Idaho, Montana, and several Canadian provinces on the morning of August 2, 2026, when NASA’s Terra satellite captured this image. Smoke from the fire was expected to cause unhealthy to very unhealthy air quality in Chelan to the east and unhealthy conditions in Leavenworth and Wenatchee to the south, according to a smoke outlook issued by the U.S. Interagency Wildland Fire Air Quality Response Program. Widespread smoke from these and the other fires in the state combined to produce very unhealthy air quality in parts of the two counties.

items.title: A Bare Summer for Barnes Ice Cap
items.short_description: The expanse of glacial ice on Canada’s Baffin Island lost its snow cover quickly and early in summer 2026, revealing a network of melt features.
items.abstract: The expanse of glacial ice on Canada’s Baffin Island lost its snow cover quickly and early in summer 2026, revealing a network of melt features. By summer, that snow melts back, and the ice cap transforms in texture, its bare ice dotted with turquoise ponds and its surface threaded with meltwater channels. By mid-July, its snow cover was effectively gone—“the earliest it has been this bare,” said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College, who has monitored the ice cap using images from Landsat satellites and, when possible, field observations. Once snow cover melts away and bare ice is exposed, melting speeds up in the Arctic summer sunshine. The early snow loss and return of meltwater channels in 2026 means that meltwater runoff is starting earlier too, with implications for the ice cap's mass balance.
